title: The houses, the farm, and the standards we keep
vimeoName: Belong School · Module 6 · The Houses & The Standards

segments.text: If you're going to represent Craveral, you need to know Craveral properly, in
detail, the way you know your own home. This module is a tour.
Some of this you know. I want all of you to know all of it.
Start with the big picture. Nine hectares, 38 independent houses
arranged in clusters, three main clusters of houses, plus studios closer to the
central facilities. Only 4% of the land is built.
The rest is working farm, orchards, vegetable gardens, animals, and pine forest,
all stitched together by those raised wooden walkways. The houses.
Every one is independent, minimalist but warm, each with its own character, and all
of them share the same DNA: sustainability, local craftsmanship, homage to
Portuguese heritage. Every unit has a proper equipped kitchen, organic amenities,
air conditioning, and a private terrace with table and armchairs. Pets are welcome.
This matters to more guests every year, and we do it properly, not grudgingly.
Know your unit types. The studios, 40 square meters, sleep two.
The farmhouses, 64 square meters, one bedroom, sleep four.
The farm lofts, also 64 square meters, sleep two.
We wood the core in cherry and oak, and part of the Craveu Cluster, which has its
own private pool for its guests. The two-bedroom houses, 85
square meters, sleep four comfortably, up to six.
With the wood-burning stove in the living room, the farmer's house, two bedrooms,
damn furniture, SMEG kitchen, two outdoor decks, and the owner's house.
We wood, our signature. 85 square meters, Essent mattress, cork
bath, a small library. The house I'd show a magazine.
Why am I making you learn square meters and bed widths?
Because confidence sells, and vagueness kills.
When a guest asks, "Would the two-bedroom work for us with the kids?" The team
member who answers precisely, "Yes.
And if the kids are small, the sofa bed in the living room gives you flexibility.
The second bedroom can be twins or a double.
Tell me which." That person has just created trust.
Trust is the currency of this whole business. The shared spaces.
Three swimming pools. The big outdoor one, 24 by 9 meters, proper laps.
The heated indoor pool, 12 by 5, with the glass-front sauna beside it.
And the children's outdoor pool. The wellness deck, raised in the pine forest.
Outdoor sauna, hot tub, cold plunge. A real thermal circuit. The gym.
The nature interpretation center, wood and glass in the pines, which hosts yoga
twice a week, retreats, workshops, meetings, and seats up to 50 for a banquet, or
80 standing. The terrace with the fire pits between the restaurant and the pool,
and the playground area, which can host events up to 300 banquet style.
The farm. This is not decoration, and I need everyone to internalize that.
The farm provides most of what our kitchen serves.
Over 70% of the restaurant's ingredients are grown on-site.
Vegetable gardens, fruit orchards, herbs, free-range eggs.
Guests are invited to walk it, to harvest seasonal produce, to meet the animals, to
cook what they pick in their own kitchenette if they like. Nothing is wasted.
Everything is connected. Field to fork, earth to plate, scraps to compost,
compost to field. When a guest asks a farm question you can't answer, that's fine.
Walk them to someone who can, and then learn the answer yourself for next time.
The shop. Local wines, artisanal rums, small batch honey, jams, olive oil,
herbal teas, natural soaps, and body oils made nearby with traditional methods.
Comfortable clothing inspired by farm life.
The shop is the territory, condensed and portable.
Every product has a story and a producer. Learn a few of them.
This honey comes from a producer 20 minutes from here, turns a souvenir into a
relationship. And the laundry in São Teotónio, which serves our operation and
serves the village. I love that our back of house is also a service to our
neighbors. That's circular economy in its plainest clothes.
Now, standards. Let me tell you how I think about them.
A standard is a promise we've made to every future guest based on what we've
delivered to past ones. When housekeeping prepares a house, they're not cleaning a
room. They're keeping a promise. The guest paid for the Craveral of the photographs
and the reviews. Every detail that's right, the bed impeccable, the
kitchen spotless, the terrace inviting, the amenities complete, keeps the promise.
Every detail that's wrong breaks it. Just a little.
And broken promises accumulate silently.
A guest rarely complains about the small stuff.
They just quietly downgrade their opinion.
And then one day, they book somewhere else, and we never learn why.
So my rule is simple: Details are not small.
In our world, details are everything, because our whole promise is care.
A farm hotel that preaches love of the land but has a dirty pool filter or a
burnt-out bulb on a walkway is a contradiction the guest feels immediately,
even if they can't articulate it. Coherence between what we say and what we do
is the highest standard we have. And when you see something wrong that isn't
your job, a fallen branch on a walkway, a smudged window, litter near the
pool, there are two kinds of team members.
The one who thinks, "Someone should fix that," and the one who fixes it or reports
it within the hour. Craveral was built by the second kind. Be the second kind.
Next module, the farm table and everything we serve.
The plate where the whole philosophy lands.
